content: At the local level, Chapter 6 provides additional guidance on unique identifier (UID) systems. Prioritizing HIV Prevention Services HIV prevention programs and service providers must understand the specific vulnerabilities and risks of HIV acquisition faced by the individuals and communities they serve. This includes considering their values and preferences. It is essential to recognize how societal attitudes—based on factors such as age, gender, ethnicity, disability, and the criminalization of key populations—can increase the risk of HIV acquisition and limit access to prevention services. Several factors influence whether individuals are at substantial risk of acquiring HIV. These include their own or their partners’ sexual and drug-using behaviors, whether their sexual partners are living with HIV, and if those partners are virally suppressed. Risk levels can change over time due to changes in behaviors, partnerships, or partners’ viral suppression status. Additionally, the overall HIV prevalence and incidence in the geographic area where individuals live play a significant role. In areas with high HIV prevalence or low viral suppression, even lower-risk behaviors may carry a relatively higher risk of HIV acquisition. Combining population-level data on ageand gender-specific HIV incidence or prevalence with individual-level risk differentiation can help prioritize prevention services. National HIV programs or public health jurisdictions should review the latest epidemiological data at national, regional, and municipal levels to identify subpopulations with higher HIV incidence or prevalence that may benefit from prioritized prevention services. Globally, key populations—such as men who have sex with men, sex workers, people who inject drugs, transgender and gender-diverse individuals, and people in prisons or other closed settings—are disproportionately affected by HIV. Some individuals may have overlapping vulnerabilities that multiply their risk, such as sex workers or transgender individuals who also inject drugs. Other groups at substantial risk include adolescent girls and young women, particularly in southern and eastern Africa, and serodiscordant couples where the partner with HIV is not virally suppressed. However, not all individuals within these groups are at substantial risk at all times. Identifying individuals who may benefit from prevention services but do not seek them out can be challenging. Prioritizing HIV prevention services and associated monitoring systems for populations and individuals who may benefit most can enable providers to efficiently follow up with those testing HIV-negative, as the resources required to follow up with large numbers of HIV-negative individuals are substantial. In all settings, a process for differentiating individuals at substantial risk of HIV and who may benefit from prevention services can be integrated into health information systems (HIS). This aids providers in offering appropriate services and follow-up. Prevention prioritization tools, such as risk differentiation or risk assessment questionnaires, can help individuals who may be unaware of their vulnerability or uncomfortable discussing it with healthcare workers to start conversations about HIV prevention. Understanding Person-Centered HIV Prevention Needs Conversations between service providers and clients during consultations are crucial for understanding individual HIV prevention needs. These discussions may occur before or after HIV testing, during sexual health consultations, or when providing prevention services. However, discussing sensitive topics such as sexual behaviors, sexual identity, and drug use can be uncomfortable for both clients and providers, especially when these behaviors are stigmatized or criminalized. Ensuring privacy and confidentiality is key, and community-led services and peer workers play an important role in creating trusted and safe environments for these conversations. Providers should offer prevention interventions to all individuals who request them, even if they are unwilling to discuss their reasons for concern. Some individuals may not feel comfortable discussing HIV due to fear of stigma or reluctance to disclose sexual or drug-using behaviors. Young people, in particular, may be hesitant to disclose sexual activity in settings with restrictive laws on adolescent access to sexual and reproductive health services. In such cases, the fact that an individual has self-identified as needing services should be recorded in the data system without requiring additional information. Sometimes, individuals may underestimate their own vulnerability to HIV, even when they have known risk factors such as a recent sexually transmitted infection (STI). Prevention prioritization tools, which include a series of questions about HIV risk factors, can help individuals recognize their risk and initiate conversations about prevention. These tools can also be self-administered, allowing individuals to assess their own risk and motivate those at risk to protect themselves. Questions for HIV Prevention Prioritization Questions to assess a person’s risk factors for HIV can serve as a programmatic counseling tool to expand access to prevention. Validated tools have been developed for different populations, such as men who have sex with men in the United States, pregnant women and heterosexual serodiscordant couples in eastern Africa, and adolescent girls and women of reproductive age in South Africa. For example, a nine-question tool in Zimbabwe identified 77% of adolescent girls and young women who acquired HIV or HSV-2 within 12 months. However, most tools have only moderate ability to distinguish individuals at high risk of HIV acquisition. Providers should offer prevention interventions to all individuals who request them, regardless of their responses to risk assessment questions. In high-prevalence settings, healthcare providers can use risk factor questions to initiate conversations about HIV, prioritize prevention services, and prompt regular follow-up for individuals who may not recognize their own risk. Capturing HIV Prevention Demand in Health Data Systems Collecting individual-level data on HIV prevention needs allows for monitoring how well services meet demand. Data can be gathered from prioritization questions or during service provision and recorded in prevention data systems. This information can indicate whether an individual belongs to a key population, such as men who have sex with men, sex workers, or people who inject drugs. However, it is important to recognize the limitations of this data, as individuals may not disclose sensitive information. Individual-level data on services received, such as injecting equipment or STI treatment, can indicate ongoing demand for related services, such as HIV testing or drug dependence treatment. Since risk and prevention needs vary over time, it is important to record the date of data collection and consider this when assessing current needs. Data collected within the last three to six months is more likely to be relevant. Individual-level data may be recorded at the point of service delivery or referral. Use of Individual-Level Data for Client and Program Management Healthcare providers can use individual-level data to improve personalized management of prevention needs. Regularly reviewing data records or using automated alerts can flag follow-up actions, such as missed appointments or services. Reminders can be issued through various methods, provided individuals have consented to these contact methods. Privacy and safety should always be prioritized when contacting individuals. Electronic databases with analytic tools, such as District Health Information Software 2 (DHIS2), can generate summary reports and display information through dashboards. Longitudinal data allows for cohort-type analyses, tracking trends, and calculating person-years of follow-up to examine outcomes and intervention coverage over time.
